claimed_purpose.text: MemMachine provides persistent, multi-session memory for AI agents, enabling personalized and context-rich experiences.
Provides episodic and profile (semantic) memory management for a specific context
Open-source long-term memory layer for AI agents and LLM-powered applications
MemMachine operates as an enterprise memory platform with a hosted API
Persistent memory that survives restarts, sessions, and model changes

mechanisms.text: Forget (delete) removes events by UUID: resolves segment UUIDs for those events, resolves derivative UUIDs for those segments, deletes derivatives from the vector store first, then deletes segments from the segment store.

MemMachine has an internal long-term memory store that uses longer field names (produced_for_id, producer_role, producer_id) for filtering, distinct from the shorter names exposed in the external API.
MemMachine includes an AmazonBedrockReranker component (amazon_bedrock_reranker.py) with a score() method that scores retrieved candidates against a query, using a configurable model_id
The profile extraction prompt passes the prior profile state and a conversation history snippet, indicating a read-then-update write path for the profile/semantic store.
Episodes use created_at which conflates ingestion time with when the event occurred; proposed fix is a timestamp or time range indicating when the event occurred.
MemMachine distinguishes between at least two workflow types: a retrieval-agent workflow and a legacy episodic workflow, both covered by the evaluation toolset.
The EpisodicMemoryManager maintains a process-local cache, identified as the main scaling bottleneck for cross-replica coherence.
The server currently has no crash recovery guarantees; proposed fix is transactional or self-healing operations on restart.
Background semantic ingestion can be triggered from MCP; the reporter requests an option to disable it from that path.
Features can be deleted individually by feature ID, or in bulk by set_id with an optional filter expression.
clean command removes all services and data, implying a full store wipe rather than selective forget
Memory is scoped per session via a session_key; no cross-session sharing is present in this module.
A project in `delete` status continues to serve search results from a process-local instance cache.
Influence Strip reveals which memories are shaping each response, providing retrieval transparency
Retrieval is scoped exclusively to long-term memory, not the current session or a combined store
Episodes record who produced them and for whom, enabling producer/role and target isolation
Results are typed as a SearchResult object with an episodic_memory field, not a plain dict
Isolation is per-user, per-agent, per-group, and per-session via constructor parameters
This retrieval agent explicitly does not rewrite or mutate memory — it is read-only
Retrieval agent uses intelligent orchestration for complex multi-hop memory queries
add_memory is triggered when facts, preferences, or important context are shared
Memory persists across multiple sessions, not just within a single conversation.
Semantic memory organized via categories, tags, sets, features, and templates
Uses OpenAI API for language models and embeddings within the server
Supports multiple memory types: preferences, weaknesses, commitments
Persistence depends on Neo4j and PostgreSQL as backing stores
Memory scoped to users, sessions, or agents via MemoryContext
Persistence scoped across sessions, agents, and LLMs
Projects provide isolated memory namespaces

ledger.claim: Write path: events are segmented into segments, segments produce derivatives, derivatives are embedded and upserted into a vector store, and segment-to-derivative mappings are persisted in a segment store partition.
ledger.quote:
await self._segment_store_partition.add_segments({segment: [derivative.uuid for derivative in segment_derivatives] for segment, segment_derivatives in segments_to_derivatives.items()})
...await self._vector_store_collection.upsert(records=derivative_records)
ledger.label: measured

ledger.claim: Retrieve path: query is embedded, vector store searched for derivatives, results deduplicated to seed segments by best score, surrounding segments fetched from segment store to expand context, then optionally reranked.
ledger.label: measured

ledger.claim: Forget is a hard delete: derivatives removed from vector store, then segments removed from segment store, keyed by event UUID.
ledger.quote:
# Delete from vector DB first, then segment store.
if derivative_uuids:
    await self._vector_store_collection.delete(record_uuids=derivative_uuids)
await self._segment_store_partition.delete_segments(segment_uuids=segment_uuids)
ledger.label: measured

ledger.claim: Proposed fix queries child partition tables directly to reduce lock scope to one relation per episodic read, preserving SQLite compatibility
ledger.quote: Query the child tables directly (preferred): the partition handle already owns its key; issuing DML against `segment_store_sg_p_<key>` / `segment_store_dv_ln_p_<key>` makes every plan reference exactly one relation — no 316-way planning, 1-2 locks, immune to the generic-plan flip.
ledger.label: inferred

ledger.claim: Original store contract enforced single-process ownership per logical collection, with lifecycle ops guarded by per-process asyncio locks.
ledger.quote: safe concurrent usage on a single process" and "safe concurrent sharded usage (one node per logical collection) on multiple processes". With ownership fixed per process, lifecycle operations (create, open-or-create, delete) could be read-check-write sequences guarded by per-process `asyncio` locks
ledger.locator: section: The model the codebase was built on, and why — decision 1
ledger.label: inferred

ledger.claim: Per-tenant child tables in PostgreSQL caused lifecycle DDL deadlocks with writers and with each other at scale.

ledger.locator: section: Why the sharded model fails them — table row: Per-tenant DDL on shared PostgreSQL parents
